awd_titl_txt: Travel: NSF Student Travel Grant for 2024 ACM/IEEESymposium on Edge Computing (ACM/IEEE SEC)
awd_abstract_narration:
The proposal is to seek travel support for up to 20 students to attend the 2024 ACM/IEEE Symposium on Edge Computing (ACM/IEEE SEC) in Rome, Italy. This leading technical conference is the primary venue for presenting new research results in the area of "edge computing", a new paradigm in which the resources of a small data center are placed at the edge of the Internet, in close proximity to mobile devices, sensors, and end users, and the emerging Internet of Things (IoT). The conference will consist of technical paper presentations, panels, PhD forums, posters, and demonstrations. It will also feature keynote speeches from leading researchers and practitioners in the field.

Participation in SEC 2024 and similar conferences are valuable and important activities of the graduate school experience. It provides students with the opportunity to interact with more senior researchers, and exposes students to leading work and practical industry practices in this important area of research. This may have an important impact on career development. The goal of the funds is to support approximately 20 student participants at recognized US institutions of higher education. Funds will be dispersed with preference given to students who would not otherwise be able to attend the conference and students who are not already scheduled to present a paper, paying particular attention to diversity and relevance of the student's research interest.

This award reflects NSF's statutory mission and has been deemed worthy of support through evaluation using the Foundation's intellectual merit and broader impacts review criteria.

por.por_cntn:
This project provided travel support for students at U.S. institutions to attend the 2024 ACM/IEEE Symposium on Edge Computing (SEC) in Rome, Italy, from December 4 to 7, 2024. SEC is a leading technical conference for presenting new results in edge computing, a paradigm that places computation and data services closer to where data are generated to improve responsiveness, privacy, and reliability. The program included technical paper presentations, panels, posters, workshops, and keynote talks by prominent researchers and practitioners. By enabling student participation, the award strengthened the research pipeline in a rapidly evolving area and expanded access for students who might not otherwise have been able to attend.

This award reflects NSF's statutory mission and has been deemed worthy of support through evaluation using the Foundation's intellectual merit and broader impacts review criteria.

Over the life of the award, the project supported 14 students from diverse U.S. institutions, including public and private research universities. Examples include the Georgia Institute of Technology, Stony Brook University, the University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign, The Ohio State University, Carnegie Mellon University, Texas A&M University, the State University of New York at Binghamton, San Jose State University, the City University of New York, and William & Mary. The cohort represented a healthy mix of academic levels, primarily doctoral students at approximately 80 percent, with participation from graduate and undergraduate students, balancing deep research engagement with early talent development.

Students attended research sessions and interactive events covering topics such as AI at the edge, edge systems, privacy and security, and real-time data analytics. They engaged in structured discussions of their work and received targeted feedback from experts across academia and industry. These interactions exposed students to state-of-the-art methods and open problems, improved their scientific communication skills, and catalyzed new collaborations.

Broadening participation was a central goal. The program used an open application process, clear selection criteria, and a review committee to balance excellence with equity considerations, including first-time attendance, financial need, and alignment with conference themes. By lowering financial barriers to a premier venue, the project expanded student access to frontier knowledge and professional networks in edge computing. The result is a better prepared and more diverse next generation of researchers ready to advance technologies that make intelligent services faster, safer, and more trustworthy in everyday life.
